newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn says open to compromise in EU row on VW funds.
newsitem.headline: Bonn says open to compromise in EU row on VW funds.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt has suggested temporarily freezing controversial east German subsidies to car giant Volkswagen AG in order to settle a row with the European Commission over the funds.
VW has received 91 million marks ($61.09 million) in subsidies to encourage its investment in two plants in the East German state of Saxony, which the European Commission says are unauthorised.

In an interview to be published in this week's Der Spiegel magazine, Rexrodt said he supported Volkswagen's case but said a temporary freeze of the allegedly excess funds pending a European court ruling could form the basis for compromise.
"But that will not work without the support of the receiver of the payment. VW has not yet warmed to an idea like this," Rexrodt cautioned.

A row over funds erupted last month when Kurt Biedenkopf, state premier for the east German state of Saxony, paid out 142 million marks to Volkswagen, in defiance of European Commission complaints that the sum was too large.
A European ruling in June cleared only 540 million marks in east German subsidies for Volkswagen out of an initial plan for 780 million marks.
In an interview published in the Financial Times' weekend edition, Volkswagen chairman Ferdinand Piech insisted that the funds were paid legally.
Piech said: "We received it (the investment) legally and because we did so, we will invest it correctly. We had the choice of any location: without support, it would not have been this one."

Rexrodt, who discussed the dispute with European Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert on Friday but failed to reach a solution, said he believed the subsidy payment was justified, but "problematic and politically ... dubious".
On Friday, the economics minister said there was a strong possibility that Bonn would bring the case to the European Court of Justice.
Saxony's Biedenkopf said in an interview this weekend with the German magazine Super Illu that he would not bend on the subsidy payment, on which he said 23,000 jobs depended.
Volkswagen had threatened to pull the plug on its plans to build plants in the Saxony towns of Mosel and Chemnitz if the funds were not paid in full.
"We will fight through this," said Biedenkopf.
The Commission is due to discuss the case on September 4. Meanwhile Bonn and the Commission are to continue their talks. ($1=1.4895 Mark)
